{{Short description|Type of polyhedron with many holes}}

[[File:De divina proportione - Vigintisex Basium Planum Vacuum.jpg|thumb|[[Rhombicuboctahedron]], one of the [[Leonardo da Vinci]]'s geometrical shapes illustration in 1509 ''[[Divina proportione]]'']]
A '''Leonardo polyhedron''' is a polyhedron with a [[Platonic solid]]'s rotational symmetry and [[Genus (mathematics)|genus]] <math> g \ge 2 </math>. Here, a polyhedron is the unbounded [[2-manifold]] embedded in [[three-dimensional Euclidean space]]. The polyhedron is named after [[Leonardo da Vinci]], who illustrated geometrical shapes in [[Luca Pacioli]]'s ''[[De divina proportione]]'' in three phases: drawing Platonic solids and [[Archimedean solid|Archimedean solids]]; replacing the edges of those solids by struts, forming a [[convex polygon]], and this results in the first polyhedron with many genera; and placing each hole with the [[Skeleton (topology)|skeleton]] of a [[Pyramid (geometry)|pyramid]].{{sfnp|Bokowski|2022}}

[[Alicia Boole Stott]] discovered the first [[Regular polyhedron|regular]] Leonardo polyhedron (its property has transitivity by [[Flag (geometry)|the set consisting of vertex, edge, and face of a polyhedron]]). Similar to Leonardo's work, she began the construction with a [[4-dimensional polytope|four-dimensional polytope]], projecting to a [[Schlegel diagram]], and replacing its edges with quadrilateral-shaped struts.{{sfnmp
 | 1a1 = Stott | 1y = 1910
 | 2a1 = Bokowski | 2y = 2022
}} [[Harold Scott MacDonald Coxeter|Coxeter]] later discovered the [[regular skew polyhedron]].{{sfnp|Coxeter|1937}} [[Felix Klein]] discovered the three genera.{{sfnmp
 | 1a1 = Klein | 1y = 1879
 | 2a1 = Klein | 2y = 1884
}} Together with [[Robert Fricke]], they found the five genera of Leonardo polyhedra.{{sfnp|Klein|Fricke|1890}} Some colleagues further discovered the locally regular and the genus up to 14.{{sfnmp
 | 1a1 = Gévay | 1a2 = Wills | 1y = 2013
 | 2a1 = Bokowski | 2y = 2022
 | 3a1 = Bokowski | 3a2 = H. | 3y = 2025
}}
